archetype.name: Pocket Passer (high-volume)
archetype.definition: An 11th-year rhythm thrower who wins from a clean pocket with quick decisions and outside-the-numbers throws to his two lead receivers, and piles up volume because his defense keeps forcing shootouts.

report.headline: A volume passer living on sack avoidance while his accuracy quietly slips.
report.take:
Prescott is what he has been for most of a decade: a pocket passer whose value is decision speed, ball placement outside the numbers and a willingness to throw 40 times a game. The volume is real and structural. He ranks 8th in passing yards per game at 264.4, on a 4,495-yard pace, because the Cowboys' defense ranks 30th in EPA allowed and keeps putting him in high-total games. Five of his seven games have gone over. That is not a hot streak. It is the shape of this team.

The engine is protection and processing. He has been sacked on just 2.5% of dropbacks and turns pressure into a sack only 11.3% of the time, both first among 45 qualifiers. The line helps, ranking 5th in hit rate allowed. He also lives outside: throws left and right both return 0.245 EPA, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens have been worth 0.339 and 0.419 EPA a target, and his 22 deep attempts have produced 0.691 EPA a throw with a +10 CPOE. Add 11 red-zone touchdowns and no lost fumbles, and the result is a 0.175 EPA per dropback that ranks 14th.

The yardage efficiency tells a plainer story. His 6.78 yards per attempt and 6.86 ANY/A both rank 25th, roughly league average. The gap between those and his EPA comes from things that wobble: touchdown timing, a small deep sample and a sack rate far below anything in his career, where pressure-to-sack sat between 19% and 35% in every charted season. Underneath, his bad-throw rate has climbed to 13.6% from last year's 11.2%. The middle of the field has been dead (0.01 EPA, three interceptions), and four of his five interceptions came on intermediate throws. The Week 5-6 slide was partly the opponents: Tampa's defense now ranks 3rd and Green Bay's 12th. But his CPOE over the last three games is -4.1, and that is a real dip in accuracy, not just schedule.

The Philadelphia game showed both sides of him. Against a defense that now ranks 27th, he pushed his aDOT to 13.4 and posted +12 EPA on just 27 attempts. Against bad pass defenses he is still a top-10 producer. Against good ones, the intermediate turnovers and the dead screen game drag him toward the middle of the pack. Expect a season that looks like 2025: big volume, slightly above-average efficiency, and 10-plus interceptions.

strengths.title: Best sack avoidance in the league
strengths.body: He leads all qualifiers in both sack rate and pressure-to-sack rate. That comes from a 2.78-second average release behind a line that rarely lets him get hit. It keeps drives alive and props up his EPA. It is also well beyond his career norms, so expect some regression toward a normal sack rate. Even then, his release speed and the protection should keep him above average.

strengths.title: Outside throws to Lamb and Pickens
strengths.body: His production runs through the boundary receivers. Lamb has added 28.2 EPA on 83 targets, and Pickens has been even more efficient per target. Both sidelines return identical, strong EPA. With two receivers who win outside, this part of his game is built on personnel and should hold up.

strengths.title: Shootout-driven volume
strengths.body: With the Cowboys' defense 30th in EPA and 30th against the pass, he is throwing about 39 times a game and sits 8th in yards per game. That volume does not depend on how well he plays. It is the game script this roster creates, and it should persist all year.

concerns.title: Accuracy has slipped
concerns.body: His bad-throw rate ranks 23rd, up 2.4 points from a 2025 season where it ranked 6th. Over the last three games his CPOE is -4.1 and his interception rate is 3.3%. Part of that is Tampa and Green Bay's defenses, but the misses were there against weaker teams too. His career shows this rate swinging from year to year rather than rising steadily, which argues for partial recovery rather than decline.

concerns.title: Intermediate and middle turnovers
concerns.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards hold four of his five interceptions, on just 52.4% completions. Throws over the middle produce essentially zero EPA with three picks. Interceptions have always been his tax, with his count ranking in the bottom third most years. This is a long-running trait that will keep costing him a pick most weeks, not noise.

concerns.title: Dead weight underneath
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have cost 15 EPA, and Jake Ferguson has been a negative-EPA target on 25 looks. This is mostly a design and personnel problem, not his arm. But it limits how efficient he can be when defenses take away the boundary.

trend.note: Four solidly positive games opened the season, then he posted -3.3 and -8.4 EPA against Tampa and Green Bay before rebounding to +12 against Philadelphia. His output tracks the opponent's pass defense more than any steady rise or fall.

nextGame.headline: Arizona's leaky secondary invites another big passing day at home
nextGame.body:
This matchup fits his profile cleanly. Arizona's defense ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed and 31st in explosive passes allowed. It allows 0.869 EPA on deep throws, 27th. It also gives up 22.3 PPR points a game to quarterbacks, 31st, with the second-most touchdowns. Its run defense is respectable at 9th, so the easy path for Dallas runs through Lamb and Pickens. The Book agrees, listing Dallas -6.5 with a 54.5 total, the highest of any Cowboys game this year.

As of reports on October 25-26, Arizona listed CB Max Melton (66% of snaps), S Andrew Wingard (76%) and DT Walter Nolen III (62%) as out. Their projected returns fall on game day, so treat their status as open. If Melton and Wingard sit again, an already weak secondary gets thinner behind the corners. If Nolen sits, Arizona loses interior rush he can't easily replace. On the Dallas side, only depth players are listed: KaVontae Turpin plays 15% of snaps and OT Drew Shelton 2%. The passing core and the protection are intact.

keyMatchups.title: His deep ball vs. Arizona's soft shell
keyMatchups.body: His 22 deep attempts have been his most efficient throws. Arizona has been among the worst at defending throws of 20-plus air yards and at limiting explosive passes. Expect the aggressive version from the Philadelphia game, with a high aDOT and more shots.

keyMatchups.title: Lamb and Pickens vs. ARI corners
keyMatchups.body: Arizona ranks 30th in EPA allowed to both WR1s and WR2s. That lines up with exactly where his production lives. A thinned cornerback group, if Melton misses again, only widens the edge.

keyMatchups.title: Game script cutting late volume
keyMatchups.body: Arizona's offense ranks 19th and is down multiple running backs, so Dallas could build a lead. He has played only 7 snaps all year while leading by 9 or more. A comfortable lead could trim his fourth-quarter attempts below his usual 39. That limits the volume ceiling rather than the efficiency.

nextGame.watch: Whether the intermediate interceptions show up even against a weak secondary. A clean game here would suggest the Week 5-6 accuracy dip was mostly the opponents.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is the safest part of his outlook. A bottom-three defense means he will keep throwing near 40 times a game in high-total games, and his yardage should stay in the top-10 range. His efficiency should settle somewhat below the current 0.175 EPA per dropback. The career-best sack avoidance will likely give some of itself back, the deep-ball hit rate rests on 22 attempts, and touchdown efficiency in the red zone on sub-50% completions is hard to hold. His career interception habit argues for one pick most weeks.

The floor is solid because the protection and the two outside receivers are real. The ceiling depends on opponents: against defenses like Tampa he has looked like a league-average passer, and against weak pass defenses like Philadelphia and Arizona he looks like a top-10 one. I project roughly 250-290 passing yards a game, 1.5-2.1 touchdowns, 0.6-0.9 interceptions and 16-21 PPR points. That is a season close to his 2025 line rather than a breakout or a collapse.
swingFactors: Whether the bad-throw rate drifts back toward last year's level
How much the sack-avoidance edge regresses
Cowboys defense forcing shootouts vs. any improvement giving him leads

confidence.note: Seven games of stable role and volume, but efficiency rests on a small deep sample and an unusually low sack rate.
